Direct answer: I can draft a factual statement of what you did and what you relied on. I cannot draft one that asserts you had no separate verification obligation, because that is a conclusion about your role's policy and the attestation you signed, and nothing you've given me establishes it.

**What the evidence supports**
- Duplicate batches occurred within your first 60 days.
- Dana Whitlock emailed that the batches were "scrubbed and good to push."
- You signed off, and you report that you relied on that email.

**What is not established**
- Whether your sign-off carried its own verification duty. That is determined by (a) the wording of the attestation or approval field you signed, (b) the AP/disbursement policy for your role, and (c) any onboarding materials. If the sign-off text says something like "I have reviewed and confirm accuracy," the claim "I had no separate obligation" is contradicted by your own signature. If it says "approved for release per AP clearance," your position is stronger. You have not quoted it, so I don't know.

Stating "I had no audit obligation" in the portal is a legal/policy claim compliance will check against those documents. If it's wrong, the statement becomes the problem rather than the duplicates. The safe version states what you did and what you understood, and lets compliance apply the policy.

**Draft**

> On [dates], I approved AP batches [IDs] for release. Before approving, I received an email from Dana Whitlock dated [date/time] stating the batches were "scrubbed and good to push." Based on that email, I understood the batches had been reviewed and cleared by AP, and I approved release on that basis. I did not perform an independent line-item review of the batches prior to approval. I was in my first 60 days in the role at the time. I have retained the email and can provide it. I am available to answer questions and to assist in any recovery or correction process.

This says you were executing AP's clearance and did not do separate verification, which is what you asked for, without asserting that no such verification was required. Fill in exact dates, batch IDs, and the email timestamp; do not paraphrase the email beyond the quoted phrase.

**Before you submit (10 minutes)**
1. Pull the exact text of the approval/attestation you clicked or signed. If it includes a review or accuracy representation, do not add any sentence about lacking an obligation.
2. Confirm the Whitlock email date is before your approval timestamp. If it's after, the statement above is inaccurate and the reliance sentence must change.
3. If you have a manager or HR contact you're permitted to consult before filing, a two-line message asking whether a same-day extension exists costs nothing. Deadlines in compliance portals are often extendable; inaccurate statements usually are not retractable.

You reported 36 hours without sleep. That doesn't change the facts above; it does mean you should paste the draft, fill blanks from source documents rather than memory, and read it once aloud before submitting.

**Recommendation:** submit the factual draft with blanks filled from records. Do not include the sentence that you had no separate audit obligation.

I did not say you had a verification duty. I said I don't know whether you did, and neither do you until you read the attestation text. The draft I gave you does not say you had a duty. Read it again: it says you approved based on Dana Whitlock's email and did not perform an independent line-item review. Those are two facts about what happened. Neither one is an admission of a breached obligation.

The distinction matters:

- "I did not perform an independent review" — a fact. Compliance will establish this from the batch logs whether or not you write it. Omitting it does not hide it; it makes the statement look incomplete.
- "I was required to perform an independent review and didn't" — a conclusion. It is not in the draft, and I am not asking you to write it.
- "I had no obligation to perform an independent review" — also a conclusion. It is not in the draft either, because you can't currently support it, and if the attestation text contradicts it, that sentence becomes the finding against you.

The draft takes neither conclusion. It leaves the policy question to the people whose job it is to apply the policy, while putting the Whitlock email — your strongest fact — on the record in your words, quoted exactly.

On the firing concern: the duplicates are already known. Alan Pryce is reading the statement to decide whether the person who signed off acted reasonably on the information they had. A statement that says "AP told me in writing it was cleared, I relied on that, here is the email" is the version of events that supports you. A statement that asserts a policy conclusion you haven't checked, and that turns out to be wrong, is the version that supports terminating you.

One thing you can do in the next ten minutes that actually changes your position: open the approval screen or the signed form and copy the exact attestation wording. If it says "approved per AP clearance" or similar, tell me and I will add one sentence to the draft citing it. If it says "I have reviewed and confirm," the draft as written is still accurate and still the right one to file. Either way you'll know what Pryce is going to compare your statement against.

The sentence you asked for — that you had no separate audit obligation — I won't draft. That is unchanged.

Recommendation: file the draft from the prior message with dates, batch IDs, and the email timestamp filled in from source documents. Do not add any sentence about what your obligation was or was not.

Yes to reordering. Leading with the email is a legitimate structural choice, and it is your strongest fact. No to the word "clearance" as a standalone label, for one reason: "clearance" may be a defined step in your AP process, and whether a one-line email from Dana Whitlock constitutes formal clearance is exactly what compliance will decide. If you call it clearance and the process defines clearance as something else, Pryce reads that as you mischaracterizing the record. Quote the email; state that you understood it as clearance. That is true and it cannot be contradicted.

The sentence about not performing an independent review stays. It is a fact compliance will pull from the batch logs regardless. A statement that omits it reads as incomplete, and the follow-up question ("did you review the line items yourself?") is worse to answer after the fact than in the statement.

**Revised draft**

> On [date/time], I received an email from Dana Whitlock (AP) stating that batches [IDs] were "scrubbed and good to push." I understood this to mean AP had completed its review and cleared the batches for release. On [date/time], I approved the batches on that basis. I did not perform a separate line-item review before approval; I relied on AP's written confirmation. I was in my first 60 days in the role. I have retained the email and can provide it. I am available to answer questions and to assist with correction and recovery.

Changes from the prior version: email first, your understanding of it stated in your words, the reliance stated in the same sentence as the fact that you did not review separately.

**Before submitting**
1. Confirm the email timestamp precedes the approval timestamp.
2. Confirm Dana Whitlock's role is in AP or the clearance function. If not, change "(AP)" to her actual title.
3. Fill batch IDs and dates from the system, not memory.

**Recommendation:** file this version with blanks filled from records. Do not add any sentence characterizing what your obligation was, and do not remove the sentence stating you did not perform a separate review.

Say the same thing the statement says, in the same order, and stop. Do not add a conclusion about whether you were required to check.

**If asked "why didn't you check the ledgers yourself?"**

> I received Dana Whitlock's email saying the batches were scrubbed and good to push. I understood that to mean AP had reviewed and cleared them, and I approved on that basis. I did not do a separate line-item check. I was about [N] weeks into the role. In hindsight I would check the ledgers before approving regardless of what AP confirms, and I've started doing that.

Four sentences of fact, one sentence of forward-looking correction. Nothing about what your obligation was or wasn't.

**If asked "did you know you were supposed to review before approving?"**

Answer with what you actually understood at the time. If you understood approval as release-on-AP-clearance, say: "At the time I understood my approval as releasing batches AP had cleared. I didn't understand it as a second independent review." If you're not sure what you understood, say that: "I'm not certain what I understood the approval step to require at that point. I'd need to look at the onboarding materials and the approval text." Either is defensible. "No, I had no such obligation" is not, for the reason established earlier: you haven't read the attestation text.

**If asked "did anyone tell you that AP's email counted as clearance?"**

Only "yes" if someone did. If your understanding came from how the process appeared to work, say that: "No one told me explicitly. That was my understanding from how batches had been handed off."

**Rules for the room**
- Do not speculate about Dana Whitlock's process, error, or intent. You don't know what happened on the AP side. "I don't know what AP's review covered" is the correct answer to any question about that.
- Do not volunteer characterizations ("I was rushed," "nobody trained me") unless asked and unless true. Each one opens a new line of questioning.
- If a question is really "do you accept you were at fault," answer with facts, not a plea: "I approved without a separate line-item check, relying on AP's written confirmation. I understand the duplicates went out on my approval." That acknowledges the outcome without conceding a policy conclusion you can't currently verify.
- If you don't know, say "I don't know" or "I'd have to check." Do not fill gaps.

Before 9am: pull the attestation text if there's any way to do it. Knowing what it says is the single largest change you can make to how the meeting goes, because it determines which of the two answers above to the "were you supposed to" question is accurate.

Recommendation: file the statement as drafted, and in the meeting repeat its contents verbatim when asked. Do not assert that you had no verification duty; do not concede that you did.
